I fixed the typo in `migrations/0007_add_customers.sql`: the column is now `email` instead of `emial`. It was the only occurrence in the repo. I didn't run anything.

An EngramDB memory said never to edit an applied migration and to add a new numbered file instead. That conflicts with your new squash-before-release process, so I marked it as challenged, quoting your message as the evidence. I left its text alone because the old rule presumably applies again after the release cut.

If `0007` has already run in any environment, such as production, that database will still have the misspelled column. Editing the file won't change it, so you'd need a fix there separately.

Yes, two things were awkward.

1. **Time-bounded exceptions to a memory.** The new rule only holds "until the release cut". `challenge` marks a memory as wrong, but it can't say "suspended until the release cut, then valid again". I wanted something like an `update` parameter such as `suspended_until` or `expires_override`, or a `premise` that I could edit on the existing hazard. The alternative was to `create` a new decision memory with `supersedes`, which would retire the old rule permanently. I didn't create that decision memory, because I wasn't sure how to record the temporary scope. As a result the store now holds only a challenged hazard and no record of the new squash process.

2. **The hook's behavior after the challenge.** The PreToolUse hook still surfaced the challenged memory as a plain fact, with no indication that it was challenged. I would have wanted the hook to show the status, or to leave out challenged memories.

I also meant to call `task_complete` and `verify`, but they weren't needed for this small change.
